items.value: Low-carbon behaviour in people has to be brought about by incentivising them
items.reasoning: The passage's argument runs: at best half the required cut can come from behavioural change by individuals and households, and even that half 'would require companies and governments to provide more incentives to change'. The pivot of the paragraph is therefore that people's low-carbon behaviour depends on being incentivised. A is wrong because the passage says demand-side (household) measures can deliver at most half, not all, of the reduction. C states a means mentioned in the last clause, not the central idea. D is not in the passage at all - no subsidy to manufacturing industry is mentioned.

items.value: Only assumption I is valid - supply-side investment by companies can produce low-carbon behaviour in people
items.reasoning: Assumption I is exactly what the last sentence presupposes: incentives delivered 'through supply-side investments to make low-carbon options cheaper and more widely available' are expected to change how individuals and households behave. Assumption II overstates the passage: the text says achieving the reduction would require companies and governments to act, which is a claim about what is needed to reach the target at scale, not a claim that people are inherently 'not capable' of low-carbon behaviour on their own. The absolute wording is what makes II fail.

items.value: A circular economy - recovering and reusing materials - can be beneficial for sustainable growth
items.reasoning: The passage sets out the problem (consumption nearly quadrupled to over 100 billion tons, under 9% reused; battery metals pricey, hard to obtain, with long risky supply chains) and then draws its own conclusion: 'Reusing materials makes sense', with spent batteries going back to a factory for their ingredients to be recovered. That is the case for a circular economy, which C states. A ('not possible without'), B ('every sector... immediately') and D ('the only option... for survival') are all absolute claims the passage never makes; the passage argues that reuse makes sense, not that nothing else can work.

items.value: Only assumption II is valid - economic growth is compatible with circular use of mineral resources
items.reasoning: The passage recommends that batteries 'should go back to a factory' - a prescription about what ought to happen, not a statement that existing automobile factories already exemplify a circular economy, so assumption I is not supported. Assumption II is the premise the whole recommendation rests on: the passage notes consumption has quadrupled and still urges recovery and reuse as something that 'makes sense', which presupposes that continued economic activity and circular use of these minerals can go together.

Per-pipe rates: set X, 20 pipes fill 0.70 tank in 14 min, so 20 pipes = 0.05 tank/min and one pipe = 0.0025. Set Y, 10 pipes fill 3/8 in 6 min, so 10 pipes = 0.0625 and one pipe = 0.00625. Set Z, 16 pipes empty 0.5 in 20 min, so all 16 empty at 0.025 tank/min. With half of X shut (10 pipes = 0.025), half of Y open (5 pipes = 0.03125) and all of Z open (-0.025), the net rate is 0.025 + 0.03125 - 0.025 = 0.03125 tank/min. Time for 50% = 0.5 / 0.03125 = 16 minutes.

1 to the power n is always 1. For 2 to the power n modulo 4: n = 1 gives 2, and for every n greater than or equal to 2 the power is a multiple of 4, giving 0. So the sum leaves remainder 1 + 2 = 3 when n = 1, and remainder 1 + 0 = 1 for every n greater than or equal to 2 (check: n = 2 gives 5, remainder 1; n = 3 gives 9, remainder 1; n = 4 gives 17, remainder 1). The set of remainders is {3, 1}, so exactly 2 distinct values.

A number of the form QQQ equals Q multiplied by 111, and 111 = 3 x 37, so every such number carries a factor of 37. Also 481 = 13 x 37. Hence the HCF is 37 multiplied by the HCF of 3Q and 13. Since Q is a digit from 1 to 9, 3Q runs from 3 to 27 and is never a multiple of 13 (13 and 26 are not multiples of 3), so that inner HCF is 1. The HCF of P and 481 is therefore 37 for every admissible Q - for example, HCF(111, 481) = 37 and HCF(999, 481) = 37.

The single-digit numbers 1 to 9 occupy positions 1 to 9. The two-digit numbers 10 to 99 are 90 numbers using 180 digits, taking us to position 189. That leaves 489 - 189 = 300 digits inside the three-digit numbers, and 300 divided by 3 is exactly 100, so position 489 is the last digit of the 100th three-digit number. The 100th three-digit number is 199, whose last digit is 9.

items.value: It cannot be concluded who stole the phone
items.reasoning: As printed the item gives no rule about who is telling the truth, and without one the statements do not fix a single thief. P's 'Q stole it' and Q's 'I did not steal' contradict each other, so exactly one of those two is false; both resulting worlds survive. If P is the thief, P lies twice and Q and R speak truly throughout; if Q is the thief, only Q's own denial is false and everything else stands. Only R is ruled out, because then both P's accusation and Q's clearing of R would be false. Different unstated conventions pick different names - 'the guilty person's every statement is false' yields P, 'assume as few false statements as possible' yields Q - which is precisely why the item is under-specified. I believe this question is defective for want of a truth-telling condition; D is the only option that is literally correct on the printed text.

items.value: Both statements are correct - P v Q was a 0-0 draw and R scored 1 goal against Q
items.reasoning: P's 3 points from two matches must be a win plus a draw; R's 1 point must be a draw plus a loss. If Q's 2 points were a win plus a loss, the only draw would be P v R, forcing P to beat Q and Q to beat R - but then R's single goal falls in the Q v R match, so Q needed at least 2 goals there, exceeding Q's tournament total of 1. So Q drew both matches: P v Q and Q v R are draws and P beat R. Now the goals: P won P v R, so P's one goal is there, making P v Q a 0-0 draw (statement I). Q's one goal must then be in the drawn Q v R match, so R matched it with 1 goal against Q (statement II), leaving R with 0 in the match lost to P. Every constraint checks out, so both statements hold.

items.value: Total dependence on genetically honed crops carries a risk of food insecurity
items.reasoning: The passage's chain is: centuries of selective breeding have stripped high-value crops of genetic variations that were not immediately useful; this raises yields but leaves them 'bad for coping with changes'; and a minor or even unknown disease 'could suddenly rampage through a genetically honed crop'. That is a warning that relying on such crops threatens our food supply, which B states. A picks up only the climate half and misses the genetic-uniformity point that the passage calls 'part of the problem'. C shifts to productivity, which the passage does not treat as the issue. D prescribes replacing crops with wild varieties - a remedy the passage never mentions.

items.value: Only assumption I is valid - climate change can spread plant diseases into new areas
items.reasoning: Assumption I follows from 'there is a risk that such changes will make some plant infections more common in all climatic zones' - infections becoming common in zones where they were not is exactly a movement of diseases into new areas. Assumption II brings in the wild relatives of crops, which the passage never mentions; it speaks only of variations bred out of cultivated genomes and says nothing about studying wild relatives or about how food security might be strengthened. II is a plausible outside idea rather than something the passage assumes.

items.value: The opposition is indispensable in a democracy, for the balance of political power and for good governance
items.reasoning: The author says a statesman should 'pray never to be left without opponents', because they 'keep him on the path of reason and good sense', and closes on national unity depending on 'a sufficiently even balance of political power'. D captures both halves - indispensability and balance. A reverses the argument. B is contradicted by the closing line, which wants it to be impracticable for opposition to be revolutionary. C misreads the point: the passage is about being kept on the path of reason and good governance, not about a ruler's political survival.

Assumption I confines the need for opposition to the case of an indifferent head of government, whereas the passage treats opponents as always necessary - a wise statesman should pray never to be left without them, and even a good statesman learns from them. Assumption II is contradicted outright by the last sentence, which wants the balance of power to make it impracticable for the opposition to be 'revolutionary and irreconcilable'; the passage argues for balanced, not aggressive, opposition.

items.value: Only four of the statements are definitely true
items.reasoning: P, Q and R are siblings, S is their mother and T is their father, so S and T are the parents of the same children and form a couple (I is true), T is Q's father (III), S is P's mother (IV), and since P is called a 'brother' P is male and so is S's son (VI). Statements II and V fail on gender: nothing tells us Q is male, so 'Q is T's son' is not definite, and nothing tells us R is female, so 'R is T's daughter' is not definite either. That leaves I, III, IV and VI - four. The judgement call is statement I: co-parenthood is read as a couple by the usual convention of these relationship items, and if it were rejected the count would fall to three.

The code is the product of the alphabetical positions of the letters. NO gives 14 x 15 = 210; NOT gives 14 x 15 x 20 = 4200; NOTE gives 4200 x 5 = 21000 - all three match. So NOTES = 21000 x 19 (for S) = 399000.

P = 3T with T not 0 and P a single digit forces T in {1,2,3} and P in {3,6,9}. From Q = R+3 and S = Q+4 = R+7, S being a digit forces R in {0,1,2}, giving (R,Q,S) = (0,3,7), (1,4,8) or (2,5,9). Testing the nine combinations for all-distinct digits: T=1,P=3 rules out (0,3,7) as Q=P and (1,4,8) as R=T, leaving 35291. T=2,P=6 rules out (2,5,9) as R=T, leaving 63072 and 64182. T=3,P=9 rules out (0,3,7) as Q=T and (2,5,9) as S=P, leaving 94183. The four numbers are 35291, 63072, 64182 and 94183.

X does one-third in 6 days, so the whole in 18 days, rate 1/18; Y does one-third in 8 days, whole in 24 days, rate 1/24; Z does three-fourths in 12 days, whole in 16 days, rate 1/16. Together they do 1/18 + 1/24 + 1/16 = (8 + 6 + 9)/144 = 23/144 per day. Y alone in 8 and 2/3 days completes (26/3) x (1/24) = 13/36 = 52/144 of the work, so the three together must have done 92/144. Then n x 23/144 = 92/144 gives n = 4. Check: 4 days together = 23/36 done, leaving 13/36, which Y finishes in (13/36) x 24 = 8 and 2/3 days.

The successive differences are 2, 3, 5, 7 - the prime numbers in order. Continuing with the next primes, X = 18 + 11 = 29, and the term after it is 29 + 13 = 42, which is exactly the last term printed. That the given final term is reproduced confirms the rule, so X = 29.
